title: Why Do We Get Hiccups? | Ask Huy
question: Why do we get hiccups?
answer: A hiccup happens when your diaphragm, the dome-shaped breathing muscle under your lungs, suddenly jerks all by itself. A split second later your throat snaps shut, and the air bumping into it makes the hic sound. Things like eating fast or swallowing air can start it. Nobody knows for sure why we hiccup, but scientists think it may have started as a way to help babies burp out air so they could drink more milk.

visual.what: A bright living room. Bối jumps a little with a big HIC speech bubble, hands on her chest, while Beo points at her in surprise and Huy laughs. Hùng peeks in behind them holding a box.

parts.text: Hic! Huy, help! Hic! My body keeps making this funny noise, and I am not doing it on purpose! Hic!
Bối is making frog noises!

Ah, the hiccups! Here is a surprise. Babies can hiccup even before they are born, while they are still inside their mom's body, in a special space called the womb. And cats, dogs, rabbits and horses get hiccups too!

visual.what: Huy stands in front of a big question mark. Hùng sets down a cardboard box labelled SCIENCE BOX, and Bối and Beo cheer.

parts.text: So today we will find out what really happens inside you when you hiccup, where that hic sound comes from, and why our bodies might do this at all.
And I brought my science box, so we can see it too!
Hic! Let's go!

visual.what: A simple world map with little speech bubbles saying hic pointing to Germany, Turkey, India and Kenya. Bối stands beside it looking proud.

parts.text: I know why! My grandma says you get hiccups when someone far away is talking about you. So somebody is talking about me right now!
That is a great guess, and you are not alone. In lots of places, from Germany to Turkey to India to Kenya, people tell that same story.

visual.what: Beo imagines a tiny green frog jumping inside Bối's tummy, shown in a dreamy thought bubble. Huy laughs and points at the middle of his own chest.

parts.text: I think a tiny frog jumped in her tummy!

A frog would be a very noisy guest, Beo! These are fun ideas. But scientists found the real action is right inside your own body, just under your lungs. Nobody needs to be talking about you, and no frogs needed.
Hic! Oh. That is a little bit sad. Hic!

visual.what: Hùng holds a model made of two pink balloons for lungs sitting on an upside-down red bowl. Labels read lungs, diaphragm, belly.

parts.text: Ta-da! Two balloons for lungs, and a bowl turned upside down.
Meet the star of today's show, the diaphragm. Say it with me, DIE-uh-fram. It is a flat sheet of muscle shaped like a dome, like that upside-down bowl. It sits under your lungs and above your belly.

visual.what: A simple cut-away body outline with a red dome across the middle like a wall. Above it the heart and lungs, below it the stomach and belly parts.

parts.text: The name comes from an old Greek word that means a wall in between. And that is just what it is. Above it are your heart and lungs. Below it are your stomach and other belly parts.
A muscle wall inside me? Hic! I never knew!

visual.what: Two side-by-side pictures of a chest. Left, the dome pulls down flat and blue arrows show air rushing in as the lungs grow. Right, the dome rises and arrows show air going out.

parts.text: The diaphragm is your most important breathing muscle. When it tightens, it pulls down and gets flatter. That makes more room in your chest, so your lungs get bigger and air rushes in. When it relaxes, it moves back up and the air goes out.

visual.what: Hùng lies on a rug with a teddy bear on his belly, the teddy rising and falling. In the last moment the teddy tumbles off as Hùng laughs, and Beo catches it.

parts.text: Try this. Lie down and put a teddy on your belly. Breathe in slowly. See the teddy go up? That is your diaphragm pushing down on your belly.
The teddy is riding a wave! Up, and down!
Oops, I laughed and he fell off!

visual.what: Huy smiles at the camera next to a small picture of the red dome under two lungs, with the words Step 1.

parts.text: So here is step one. Your diaphragm is a dome-shaped muscle under your lungs, and every time it pulls down, you breathe in.

visual.what: The red dome drawn as a calm swing on the left, then on the right it jerks down suddenly with zig-zag lines and a fast blue arrow of air going in.

parts.text: Now, a hiccup. Most of the time your diaphragm moves smoothly, like a gentle swing. But in a hiccup it suddenly tightens with a quick jerk, all by itself. Whoosh! Air gets pulled in fast.

visual.what: A simple side view of a throat with two little flaps labelled vocal cords, shown open and then shut like a tiny door.

parts.text: Then, a tiny moment later, something in your throat slams shut. It is the gap between your vocal cords. Those are two little flaps in your throat that help make your voice.
There is a door in my throat?

visual.what: Blue air arrows rushing up and bumping into the shut vocal cord door, with a big HIC sound burst and a tiny stopwatch showing 0.035 seconds.

parts.text: Sort of, Beo! The air rushing in bumps into that shut door, and the bump makes the sound. Hic! The throat shuts about thirty-five thousandths of a second after the jerk. That is super, super fast.
So the hic is air crashing into a door in my throat? Hic! There it goes again!

visual.what: Bối frowns with her arms crossed, telling her body to stop. Beo does a big pretend sneeze next to her, and Huy gives a thumbs up.

parts.text: But why can't I stop it? I keep telling my body to stop!
Because a hiccup is a reflex. A reflex is something your body does without you deciding, like quickly pulling your hand away from something prickly.
Like when I sneeze! Achoo!
Yes, a sneeze is a reflex too! For hiccups, your body is the boss, not you.

visual.what: Huy beside the word HICCUP written in big bouncy letters, with a sound wave under it, and the words Step 2.

parts.text: And the word hiccup? People made it up by copying the sound. Step two. A hiccup is a sudden jerk of your diaphragm, then your throat snaps shut, and that makes the hic.

visual.what: A kitchen table with an empty noodle bowl in front of Bối. Hùng holds a fizzy drink can with a surprised face and a little HIC bubble.

parts.text: So what starts hiccups? Scientists call these triggers. Common ones are eating very fast, swallowing lots of air, fizzy drinks, spicy food, and laughing hard for a long time.
I did eat my noodles super fast. And then I laughed at your joke!
Oh no. I just drank my fizzy drink super fast. Hic!

visual.what: Zooming into the stomach to show a round air bubble sitting at the top, pressing up right under the red dome of the diaphragm.

parts.text: Hiccups often happen when a bubble of air gets into your stomach and takes up space there, right under your diaphragm.

visual.what: Little sensor dots around the stomach and diaphragm send a yellow arrow up to a glowing spot in the brain labelled hiccup center, and a red arrow comes back down to the diaphragm.

parts.text: Scientists think tiny sensors in your stomach and around your diaphragm may notice the bubble. They may send a message up to a part of your brain called the hiccup center. Then the brain sends a message back down. Jerk! Hic!

visual.what: A timeline with evenly spaced HIC marks like drum beats, and a clock showing they come a few times each minute. Beo taps a toy drum.

parts.text: Hiccups also keep a beat. The time between one hic and the next usually stays about the same, often a few each minute. And most hiccups stop all by themselves after a few minutes.
Hic, hic, hic! Like a drum!
So my hiccups have their own song!

visual.what: Huy next to a small picture of an air bubble under the diaphragm, with the words Step 3.

parts.text: Step three. Things like eating fast or swallowing air can make an air bubble in your belly, and scientists think that bubble may help set off the hiccup reflex.

visual.what: Bối throws her hands up, puzzled. Huy scratches his chin thoughtfully next to a big question mark.

parts.text: But wait. Why would a body even want hiccups? They are useless! Hic!
Great question, and here is an honest answer. Scientists do not know for sure. But they have some clever ideas.

visual.what: A baby drinking from a bottle, with a cut-away tummy showing milk at the bottom and a small air bubble taking up room at the top.

parts.text: The main idea is about babies. When a baby drinks milk, it has to suck, swallow and breathe all at once. That is tricky, so some air sneaks into the tummy. And air takes up room where milk could go.

visual.what: In the baby's cut-away body, the throat door shuts and an arrow pulls the air bubble up from the tummy and out of the mouth as a small burp cloud, leaving more room for milk.

parts.text: Here is the clever part. A hiccup shuts the throat and makes a pull inside the chest. That may tug the air bubble up and out of the mouth, like a burp. Now there is more room for milk!
A hiccup is a burp helper?
Babies go burp! Hee hee!

visual.what: A line from baby to child to grown-up with fewer HIC bubbles as they get older. Beside it, a group of mammals, a cat, a dog, a horse and a rabbit, each with a milk drop.

parts.text: Some clues fit this idea. Babies hiccup a lot, and we hiccup less as we grow older. And hiccups have only been described in mammals, the animals that feed their babies milk.

visual.what: A tadpole in a pond gulping water and air across its gills, next to a child with a HIC bubble. Bối crouches like a frog.

parts.text: Some scientists have a second idea. Hiccups might be left over from long, long ago. Tadpoles gulp water and air across their gills with a simple movement a bit like a hiccup. Maybe our bodies kept an old trick.
So maybe I am hiccuping like a tadpole! Ribbit! Hic!

visual.what: Huy next to a small picture of a baby giving a tiny burp, with the words Step 4.

parts.text: Step four. Nobody knows for sure why we hiccup, but scientists think it may have helped babies burp out air so they could drink more milk.

visual.what: Hùng sits by a wall clock, still hiccuping from his fizzy drink. Bối makes a pencil mark on paper for each hic while Beo watches the clock hand.

parts.text: Here is a safe check you can try. Next time you have hiccups, look at a clock and count your hics for one minute. Make a little mark for each one. Is the time between them about the same?
Good thing I still have mine. Hic!
I have five marks in one minute for Hùng! Hic! And six for me!

visual.what: Hùng holds a glass of cold water and then hugs his knees, shown as two little pictures, while Huy points to a clock and smiles.

parts.text: People all around the world have tricks to stop hiccups, like sipping cold water or pulling your knees up to your chest. But scientists say no trick has been proven to work best. Usually the easiest cure is just to wait.
Then I will wait!

visual.what: A thought bubble shows a big brown horse in a flower field with a HIC bubble, its shoulders jumping and flowers wobbling. Below, Bối and Hùng look surprised as their hiccups stop.

parts.text: Now imagine if a horse got hiccups. Horses really can! Picture a big horse in a field going hic, with its shoulders giving a little jump each time.
The flowers would wobble!
Wait. Listen. My hiccups stopped! All by themselves!
Mine too! Waiting worked!

visual.what: Huy beside a simple three-picture strip, the diaphragm jerking down, the throat door shutting, and a HIC bubble, plus a baby burping.

parts.text: So, why do we get hiccups? Your diaphragm, the breathing muscle under your lungs, suddenly jerks. Then your throat snaps shut, and the air bumping into it goes hic. Scientists think it may have started as a way to help babies burp.

visual.what: A calendar flipping from 1922 to 1990 next to a big number reading about 68 years and about 430 million hics. Bối stares with wide eyes.

parts.text: And here is a fun fact. A man in America named Charles Osborne had hiccups for about sixty-eight years! That is a world record, about four hundred and thirty million hiccups. Do not worry, that is very, very rare.
Sixty-eight years! Mine lasted about five minutes, and that felt long!

visual.what: Bối gives a big yawn, Beo copies her, and Hùng yawns too. Huy waves next to a red subscribe button that says Ask Huy.

parts.text: All that hiccuping made me sleepy. Ahhh. Huy, why do we yawn?
Me too. Ahhh.
Ooh, that is a great question for next time! Subscribe to Ask Huy so you do not miss it, and keep asking questions. See you soon!

facts.claim: Hiccups have been observed before birth, in the womb.
Cats, rabbits, dogs and horses (and rats) get hiccups.
In many traditions (German, Turkish, Indian, some tribes in Kenya and others) people say hiccups happen when someone not present is talking about you.
The diaphragm is a dome-shaped sheet of muscle below the lungs, separating the chest (heart and lungs) from the belly.
The word diaphragm comes from an Ancient Greek word meaning partition (a wall in between).
The diaphragm is the most important breathing muscle; when it contracts it pulls down, the chest gets bigger and air is drawn into the lungs; when it relaxes the air goes out.
A hiccup is a sudden tightening of the diaphragm that pulls air in, followed by the throat closing, which makes the hic sound.
The closing is of the glottis, the space between the vocal cords, about 35 milliseconds after the diaphragm contracts.
A hiccup is a reflex, an action the body does without trying.
A sneeze and pulling your hand away from something sharp are reflexes.
The word hiccup was created by imitating the sound.
Common triggers include eating quickly, swallowing air, fizzy (carbonated) drinks, spicy food and laughing for a long time.
Hiccups often happen when a bubble of air forms below the diaphragm and takes up space in the belly.
Under the leading hypothesis, sensors in the stomach, esophagus and under the diaphragm trigger a hiccup center in the brain, which makes the breathing muscles contract.
Hiccups are rhythmic, often several per minute, and usually end on their own after a few minutes.
Why people hiccup is not known for sure.
A leading theory is that hiccups help young mammals drink milk by burping out air swallowed while suckling, making room for more milk.
Babies hiccup a lot, hiccups become less frequent with age, and hiccups are only described in mammals, which feed their young milk.
Another idea is that hiccups are left over from amphibian breathing; tadpoles gulp air and water across their gills with a reflex similar to hiccuping.
Remedies suggested include sipping ice-cold water and pulling the knees up to the chest, but no treatment is known to be especially effective; hiccups are normally waited out.
Charles Osborne of America had hiccups for 68 years (1922 to 1990), a Guinness World Record, an estimated 430 million hiccups.
Long-lasting hiccups are rare.

description: Why do we hiccup, and where does that funny hic sound come from? Huy, his helper Hùng, Bối and little Beo look inside the body to meet the diaphragm, find out what sets hiccups off, and hear the clever idea scientists have about why hiccups exist. It's a gentle, science-checked explainer for kids aged 6 to 12, with a safe hiccup-counting activity to try at home.
